title: 02 — Infrastructure & Platform
html:
02 — Infrastructure & Platform

Scope: the machine, the OS, the container, the cluster, the pipeline, the cloud. Everything between "my code compiles" and "it serves users reliably at 3am on a Sunday".

1. The OS layer — what your process actually is

1.1 Process, thread, and the resources they own

┌──────────────────────── Process (isolation boundary) ─────────────────────┐
│  Virtual address space      Handles/FDs        Security token             │
│  ┌───────┬───────┬───────┐  sockets, files     user, groups, privileges   │
│  │ Code  │ Heap  │ Stack │  pipes                                          │
│  │(text) │ (GC)  │ /thread│                                                │
│  └───────┴───────┴───────┘                                                 │
│   Thread 1        Thread 2        Thread N   ← share heap+handles,          │
│   own stack       own stack       own stack     own stack + registers       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Process Thread
Memory Isolated virtual address space Shared heap, own stack (~1 MB reserved on Windows, 8 MB virtual on Linux)
Crash blast radius Contained Kills the whole process
Creation cost ~ms ~µs–100s of µs
Communication IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) Shared memory (needs synchronisation)
Use when Fault isolation, different privilege, different runtime Concurrency inside one app

Why this matters: a thread is not free. 1000 threads = ~1 GB of stack reservations + context-switch churn. This is the entire argument for async/await and event loops: don't hold a thread while waiting on I/O (see file 12).

1.2 Virtual memory

The MMU maps virtual pages (4 KB typically) to physical frames. Consequences:

  • Page fault: touching an unmapped page → OS loads it. Soft faults are cheap (page already in RAM). Hard faults hit disk → 1000× slower. Sustained hard faults = thrashing; the machine appears frozen while CPU is idle.
  • Memory is lazily committed. top/Task Manager shows RSS/working set (resident) vs virtual (reserved). A .NET process reserving 2 GB of virtual address space isn't using 2 GB of RAM.
  • The OOM killer (Linux) picks a victim by score when memory is exhausted. In containers it kills your process with exit code 137 and no stack trace — the classic "pod restarted, no logs" mystery. ⚠️ Always check kubectl describe pod for OOMKilled.
  • Swap trades latency for capacity. On servers, swap usually turns a fast crash into a slow, undiagnosable degradation. Kubernetes disables it by default for exactly this reason.

1.3 System calls and the user/kernel boundary

Your code runs in user mode; anything touching hardware (file, socket, timer, memory map) traps into the kernel. A syscall costs ~100 ns–1 µs plus cache pollution. This is why:

  • Buffered I/O exists (one syscall for 64 KB, not 64k syscalls for 1 byte).
  • epoll/kqueue/IOCP exist (one syscall to wait on thousands of sockets — the foundation of every async runtime).
  • Zero-copy (sendfile, Span<T> over pooled buffers) matters for high-throughput paths.

🧪 Observe it: Linux strace -c -p <pid> (syscall histogram); Windows: Process Monitor / ETW / dotnet-counters.

1.4 The tools you must be fluent in

Question Linux Windows / PowerShell
What's using CPU? top, htop, pidstat 1 Get-Process \| Sort CPU -Desc \| Select -First 10
What's using memory? free -m, ps aux --sort=-rss Get-Process \| Sort WS -Desc
Disk I/O iostat -xz 1, iotop Get-Counter '\PhysicalDisk(*)\*'
Open files/sockets lsof -p <pid>, ss -tanp Get-NetTCPConnection, Handle.exe
What's this process doing? strace, perf top, /proc/<pid>/ ETW, PerfView, dotnet-trace
Who is listening on :5000? ss -lntp \| grep 5000 Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 5000
Logs journalctl -u svc -f Get-EventLog, Get-WinEvent

The 60-second Linux triage (Netflix's checklist) — run these in order on a sick box:

uptime            # load averages: trend over 1/5/15 min
dmesg | tail      # OOM kills, disk errors, TCP drops
vmstat 1          # r (runnable) > CPUs = CPU saturation; si/so = swapping
mpstat -P ALL 1   # per-core imbalance
pidstat 1         # per-process CPU over time
iostat -xz 1      # await, %util per device
free -m           # buff/cache is not "used"
sar -n DEV 1      # network throughput
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 # retransmits, resets
top               # confirm the suspect

2. Containers

2.1 What a container actually is

Not a VM. A container is a normal Linux process with three kernel features applied:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Container
      P[Your process]
    end
    P --> NS["<b>Namespaces</b> — what it can SEE<br/>pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup"]
    P --> CG["<b>cgroups</b> — what it can USE<br/>cpu, memory, io, pids"]
    P --> UFS["<b>Union filesystem</b> — what it RUNS ON<br/>layered read-only images + writable layer"]
VM Container
Isolates Hardware (own kernel) Process view (shared kernel)
Boot 10s of seconds Milliseconds
Overhead 100s of MB ~ the process itself
Security boundary Strong Weaker — a kernel exploit escapes. Use gVisor/Kata/Firecracker for hostile multi-tenancy
Density 10s per host 100s–1000s

⚠️ Shared kernel means: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. On Windows, Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM (WSL2). Windows containers exist but must match the host kernel version family (process vs Hyper-V isolation).

2.2 Images and layers

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer; layers are content-addressed and cached. Order instructions from least- to most-frequently-changing or you invalidate the cache on every build.

# Multi-stage build: ASP.NET Core + Angular, production-shaped
# ---- build Angular ----
FROM node:22-alpine AS web
WORKDIR /src
COPY ClientApp/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                                   # cached unless lockfile changes
COPY ClientApp/ ./
RUN npm run build -- --configuration production

# ---- build .NET ----
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0 AS api
WORKDIR /src
COPY *.sln .
COPY src/Api/*.csproj src/Api/
COPY src/Domain/*.csproj src/Domain/
RUN dotnet restore                           # cached unless csproj changes
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish src/Api/Api.csproj -c Release -o /app \
    --no-restore /p:UseAppHost=false

# ---- runtime ----
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:9.0-alpine AS final
RUN adduser -D -u 10001 appuser              # never run as root
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=api /app .
COPY --from=web /src/dist/browser ./wwwroot
USER 10001
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080 \
    DOTNET_gcServer=1
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health/ready || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Api.dll"]

Image hygiene rules:

  1. Multi-stage — SDK image (~800 MB) never ships; runtime image (~110 MB, or ~30 MB with Alpine + trimming) does.
  2. Pin base image digests in regulated environments (FROM image@sha256:...).
  3. Non-root user, read-only root filesystem where possible.
  4. .dockerignore — excluding bin/, obj/, node_modules/, .git often cuts build context by 90%+.
  5. No secrets in layers. RUN --mount=type=secret or inject at runtime. A deleted file in a later layer is still in the image history.
  6. Scan (Trivy, Grype, Defender) in CI and fail on critical CVEs.
  7. One process per container — the container is the supervision unit. Need a sidecar? Run a second container.

2.3 Container resources and .NET

docker run --cpus=2 --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g myapi
  • cgroup CPU limits are enforced by throttling within a 100 ms period. A limit of 0.5 CPU means the process is frozen for 50 ms of every 100 ms once it exhausts its quota → p99 latency spikes that look like GC pauses but aren't. 🧪 Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total.
  • Modern .NET is cgroup-aware: GCHeapHardLimit defaults to 75% of the container memory limit, and Environment.ProcessorCount reflects the CPU limit. Older .NET Framework / early Core did not — cause of countless OOMKills.
  • ⚠️ Requests vs limits (Kubernetes): requests = scheduling guarantee, limits = enforcement ceiling. Setting memory limit == request is standard (Guaranteed QoS). Setting a CPU limit is often counter-productive — CPU is compressible; throttling hurts latency more than the noisy-neighbour risk. Common expert guidance: always set memory limits, usually set CPU requests only.

3. Kubernetes — the mental model

3.1 Architecture

flowchart TB
    subgraph CP["Control plane"]
        API[kube-apiserver<br/>the only thing that talks to etcd]
        ETCD[(etcd<br/>desired + actual state)]
        SCH[kube-scheduler<br/>picks a node]
        CM[controller-manager<br/>reconciliation loops]
        API <--> ETCD
        SCH --> API
        CM --> API
    end
    subgraph N1["Node"]
        KL[kubelet] --> CR[containerd]
        KP[kube-proxy<br/>iptables/IPVS rules]
        POD1[Pod: app + sidecar]
    end
    API <--> KL
    API <--> KP
    U[kubectl / CI] --> API

The one idea that explains everything: the reconciliation loop. You declare desired state; controllers continuously diff desired vs actual and act. Nothing is imperative. This is why kubectl apply is idempotent, why a deleted pod comes back, and why "I fixed it by hand on the node" never sticks.

3.2 Objects you must know

Object Purpose Notes
Pod 1+ containers sharing network namespace + volumes Smallest deployable unit. Ephemeral — never create directly in prod
ReplicaSet Keeps N pod replicas Managed by Deployment; you rarely touch it
Deployment Declarative rollout of stateless pods RollingUpdate with maxSurge/maxUnavailable; kubectl rollout undo
StatefulSet Stable identity + stable storage Ordered start/stop, pod-0..n-1, per-pod PVC. For databases, Kafka, anything with identity
DaemonSet One pod per node Log shippers, node exporters, CNI
Job / CronJob Run to completion / on schedule Set backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, concurrencyPolicy
Service Stable virtual IP + DNS for a pod set ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer, Headless (clusterIP: None → DNS returns pod IPs, needed for StatefulSets/gRPC LB)
Ingress / Gateway API L7 HTTP routing into the cluster Ingress is legacy-ish; Gateway API is the successor
ConfigMap / Secret Config and credentials Secrets are base64, not encrypted, unless you enable encryption-at-rest + RBAC. Prefer external secret stores
PVC / PV / StorageClass Persistent storage claim/binding/provisioner ReadWriteOnce is the common (single-node) access mode
HPA / VPA / KEDA Autoscale by CPU/memory / right-size / scale by queue depth KEDA is what you want for queue-driven workers, incl. scale-to-zero
NetworkPolicy Pod-level firewall Default is allow-all; you must opt into deny
PodDisruptionBudget Minimum available during voluntary disruption Without it, a node drain can take your whole service down

3.3 A production-shaped Deployment

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: orders-api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }   # no capacity loss during deploy
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: orders-api } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45      # > your longest in-flight request
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      topologySpreadConstraints:             # survive a zone loss
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-api } }
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry/orders-api@sha256:...
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          env:
            - name: ConnectionStrings__Db
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: orders-secrets, key: db } }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "512Mi" }         # memory limit yes, CPU limit no
          startupProbe:                            # protects slow starts
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
            failureThreshold: 30
            periodSeconds: 2
          livenessProbe:                           # restart if wedged
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:                          # remove from LB if not ready
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop: { exec: { command: ["sleep", "5"] } }   # let endpoints propagate
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }

⚠️ The graceful-shutdown race everyone gets wrong. When a pod is deleted, SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen concurrently and endpoint propagation is eventually consistent. Without the preStop: sleep 5, kube-proxy on some node may still route to a pod that has already stopped accepting → 502s on every deploy. The correct sequence is: preStop sleep (drain window) → app stops accepting new work → finishes in-flight → exits before terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

In ASP.NET Core, honour it:

builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o =>
    o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));   // default is 5s — too short

3.4 Kubernetes failure modes cheat-sheet

Symptom Likely cause Check
CrashLoopBackOff App exits at startup (config/secret missing, port in use) kubectl logs pod --previous
OOMKilled (exit 137) Memory limit too low or a leak kubectl describe pod; compare limit with GC heap
ImagePullBackOff Bad tag, private registry auth, rate limit describe events
Pending forever No node fits requests / no PV / taints describe pod → scheduler events
Random 502s during deploy Missing preStop / readiness / maxUnavailable > 0 §3.3
Works via port-forward, not via Ingress Service selector mismatch, wrong port name, ingress class kubectl get endpoints svc — empty = selector bug
gRPC only hits one pod ClusterIP is L4; h2 multiplexes on one connection Headless service + client-side LB, or a mesh
DNS slow/intermittent CoreDNS under-provisioned, ndots:5 search-domain amplification Add dnsConfig ndots: 1, use FQDNs with trailing dot

When not to use Kubernetes: a handful of services, one team, predictable load. The operational surface (upgrades, CNI, CSI, RBAC, cost) is a full-time job. Azure App Service / Container Apps / ECS Fargate / Cloud Run give you 80% of the benefit at 10% of the cost. Choose k8s when you need multi-tenant scheduling, complex networking, or genuine portability — not because it's on the CV list.

4. Infrastructure as Code

Why: the alternative — clicking in a portal — is unreviewable, unrepeatable, and undocumented. IaC makes infrastructure a code artifact: diffed in PRs, versioned, rolled back, and reproducible in a second environment.

Tool Model Best for
Terraform / OpenTofu Declarative HCL, provider-agnostic, state file Multi-cloud, most common default
Bicep / ARM Declarative, Azure-native, no state file (Azure is the state) Azure-only shops (likely your case)
Pulumi Real languages (C#/TS/Python) Teams that want types + loops + tests
CloudFormation/CDK AWS-native AWS-only
Ansible Procedural config management VM configuration, not resource provisioning
Helm / Kustomize K8s manifest templating / overlays Cluster workloads

Rules:

  • State is precious. Remote backend with locking (Azure Storage + blob lease, S3 + DynamoDB). Never commit state; it contains secrets.
  • Plan in PR, apply on merge. The plan output is the review artifact.
  • Modules per environment, not copy-paste. Parameterise; don't fork.
  • Never mutate by hand — drift makes the next apply destructive. If you must hotfix, import it back immediately.
  • ⚠️ terraform destroy/apply on a shared state can delete a database. Guard prod with prevent_destroy, required approvals, and separate state per environment.

5. CI/CD

5.1 Pipeline anatomy

flowchart LR
    PR[PR opened] --> L[Lint + format]
    L --> B[Build]
    B --> UT[Unit tests + coverage gate]
    UT --> SEC[SAST + dependency + secret scan]
    SEC --> IT[Integration tests<br/>Testcontainers]
    IT --> PKG[Build image, sign, push<br/>immutable tag = git sha]
    PKG --> DEV[Deploy dev - auto]
    DEV --> E2E[Smoke / E2E]
    E2E --> STG[Deploy staging - auto]
    STG --> APP{Manual approval}
    APP --> PROD[Deploy prod<br/>canary → progressive]
    PROD --> VER[Verify SLOs, auto-rollback on breach]

Non-negotiables:

  • Build once, promote the same artifact. Rebuilding per environment means prod runs untested bits. Configuration is injected, not baked.
  • Immutable, traceable tags: myapi:1.4.7-abc1234, never :latest in a deployment manifest.
  • Fast feedback: PR pipeline under ~10 minutes or people stop reading it. Parallelise; move slow suites to a post-merge/nightly stage.
  • Secrets from a vault via OIDC federation, not long-lived credentials in CI variables.
  • Every pipeline is idempotent and re-runnable.

5.2 Deployment strategies

Strategy How Cost Rollback Use when
Recreate Stop old, start new Downtime Redeploy Dev, or when versions can't coexist (breaking schema)
Rolling Replace N at a time None Roll forward/back gradually Default for stateless services
Blue/green Two full environments, flip the router 2× infra Instant (flip back) High-risk releases, need instant rollback
Canary 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, gated on metrics Small Stop and shift back Anything user-facing at scale
Shadow / mirror Duplicate real traffic to the new version, discard responses Extra compute N/A Validating a rewrite under real load
Feature flags Deploy dark, enable per cohort Flag debt Toggle off (seconds) Decouples deploy from release — the highest-leverage practice here

The rule that makes all of them work: every change must be backward compatible for one version. Expand → migrate → contract:

  1. Expand: add the new column/endpoint/field, nullable/optional. Deploy.
  2. Migrate: dual-write, backfill, switch reads. Deploy.
  3. Contract: remove the old path — only after nothing references it.

⚠️ Skipping this is why "we can't roll back the deploy, the migration already ran".

6. Cloud primitives (Azure-first, with equivalents)

Concern Azure AWS GCP
VM Virtual Machines / VMSS EC2 / ASG Compute Engine / MIG
PaaS web App Service Elastic Beanstalk App Engine
Serverless containers Container Apps Fargate / App Runner Cloud Run
Functions Azure Functions Lambda Cloud Functions
Managed k8s AKS EKS GKE
Object storage Blob Storage S3 Cloud Storage
Relational Azure SQL / PG Flexible Server RDS / Aurora Cloud SQL / Spanner
NoSQL Cosmos DB DynamoDB Firestore / Bigtable
Cache Azure Cache for Redis ElastiCache Memorystore
Queue Service Bus / Storage Queue SQS Pub/Sub
Stream Event Hubs Kinesis Pub/Sub
Secrets Key Vault Secrets Manager Secret Manager
Identity Entra ID / Managed Identity IAM roles Workload Identity
CDN/WAF Front Door CloudFront + WAF Cloud CDN + Armor
Observability Azure Monitor / App Insights CloudWatch / X-Ray Cloud Operations

Choosing the compute tier — a decision that costs or saves years of toil:

flowchart TD
    A[New workload] --> B{Event-driven, spiky,<br/>short-lived?}
    B -->|Yes| F[Functions / Container Apps jobs]
    B -->|No| C{Standard HTTP service,<br/>no exotic infra needs?}
    C -->|Yes| D[App Service / Container Apps / Cloud Run]
    C -->|No| E{Many services, custom networking,<br/>platform team exists?}
    E -->|Yes| K[AKS/EKS/GKE]
    E -->|No| D

Cloud design principles that actually save money and outages:

  • Managed identity over connection strings — no secret to rotate or leak.
  • Right-size from metrics, not from fear. Then use reserved/savings plans for the steady baseline and spot/burst for the rest.
  • Multi-AZ by default; multi-region only when the business pays for it. Multi-region active-active means solving data consistency — it's a 10× complexity step, not a checkbox.
  • Tag everything (owner, env, cost-centre) or you will never explain the bill.
  • Egress is the expensive direction. Cross-region and internet egress charges dominate surprise bills; keep chatty components in one region/zone.

7. Reliability engineering (SRE) essentials

Term Definition Example
SLI A measured signal % of requests < 300 ms; % non-5xx
SLO Target for an SLI 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days
SLA Contractual promise with penalties Always looser than the SLO
Error budget 1 − SLO 99.9% ⇒ 43 min/month of allowed failure

Error budget policy is the useful part: while budget remains, ship features; when it's exhausted, feature work stops and reliability work starts. It converts "how much reliability?" from an argument into a number.

Availability maths:

SLO Downtime/month Downtime/year Implies
99% 7.2 h 3.65 d Single instance, business hours support
99.9% 43 min 8.8 h Redundancy + automated failover
99.99% 4.3 min 52 min Multi-AZ, no manual steps in recovery, canaries
99.999% 26 s 5.3 min Multi-region, cell architecture, huge cost

Serial dependencies multiply: a service that depends on 5 components each at 99.9% has a ceiling of 99.9%^5 ≈ 99.5%. This is the mathematical argument for graceful degradation and caching: reduce hard dependencies, don't just make each one better.

RTO/RPO — Recovery Time Objective (how long to restore) and Recovery Point Objective (how much data you may lose). Every system has these whether you chose them or not. A backup you haven't restored is not a backup; schedule restore drills.

Incident discipline:

  1. Mitigate first, diagnose second. Roll back, fail over, shed load. Root cause can wait; users can't.
  2. One incident commander, explicit roles, a single channel, a running timeline.
  3. Blameless postmortem within 5 business days: timeline, contributing factors, what made detection/mitigation slow, action items with owners and dates.
  4. Ask "why was this possible/undetected/slow to fix?" not "who did it?" — systems fail, people are the last line of defence, not the cause.

8. Configuration & secrets

Hierarchy (later wins), as ASP.NET Core implements it: appsettings.json → appsettings.{Env}.json → user secrets (dev) → environment variables → command line → Key Vault provider.

// Strongly-typed, validated at startup — fail fast, not at 3am on first use
builder.Services.AddOptions<PricingOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Pricing"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(o => o.TimeoutSeconds is > 0 and <= 60, "Timeout must be 1..60")
    .ValidateOnStart();

Secret rules:

  • Never in source, never in image layers, never in log output, never in a URL query string.
  • Prefer workload identity / managed identity so there is no secret at all.
  • If a secret must exist: vault-stored, access-audited, rotated on a schedule, and rotatable without downtime (support two valid keys during rotation).
  • Detect leaks: gitleaks/trufflehog in CI and as a pre-commit hook. On a real leak: rotate first, then scrub history — the credential is compromised the moment it's pushed, and rewriting history doesn't un-clone it.

9. Environments and the path to production

Environment Purpose Data Who deploys
Local Fast inner loop Seeded/synthetic (Testcontainers, LocalDB) Developer
Dev/Integration Continuous integration of everyone's work Synthetic Automatic on merge
QA/Staging Production-shaped verification Masked prod-like, same schema Automatic
Pre-prod/Canary Real traffic, small slice Production Automatic + gates
Production Users Production Approved pipeline only

Rule: staging is only useful if it is shaped like production (same topology, same versions, comparable data volume). A staging environment with 1000 rows tells you nothing about a query that dies at 50 million.

Dev environment parity, cheaply: Testcontainers gives real SQL Server/Postgres/Redis/Kafka per test run in Docker, which removes the biggest source of "works locally" — in-memory fakes that don't behave like the real engine.

10. Senior checklist — production readiness

Before a service goes live:

  • Health endpoints: /health/live (process ok) and /health/ready (dependencies ok, degradable)
  • Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM handled, preStop drain, shutdown timeout > longest request
  • Resource requests/limits set from measured usage, memory limit present
  • Horizontal scaling verified (no in-process state that breaks with N>1 — sessions, caches, schedulers, SignalR)
  • Structured logs with correlation IDs; metrics (RED); distributed traces
  • Dashboards + alerts tied to SLOs, not to raw CPU
  • Runbook: top 5 alerts, how to diagnose, how to mitigate, who to escalate to
  • Backups configured and a restore tested; RTO/RPO written down
  • Secrets in a vault, identity-based access, rotation plan
  • Rollback path proven (not "we'd roll forward")
  • Load test at 2× expected peak; know where it breaks and how it fails
  • Cost estimated and tagged
  • Zero single points of failure in the request path, or documented acceptance of each

🔍 Interview angles

  • Container vs VM? Shared kernel + namespaces/cgroups vs full hardware virtualization; trade density and speed against isolation strength.
  • What happens when you kubectl apply a Deployment? apiserver validates → persists to etcd → Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet → ReplicaSet controller creates Pods → scheduler binds pods to nodes → kubelet pulls the image and starts containers → readiness gates endpoint membership. All reconciliation loops, all eventually consistent.
  • Why do we see 502s only during deploys? Endpoint propagation races pod termination; fix with preStop drain + readiness + maxUnavailable: 0.
  • Blue/green vs canary? Blue/green optimises rollback speed at 2× cost; canary optimises blast radius with metric gating. Both need backward-compatible changes.
  • How do you decide k8s vs PaaS? Count the things k8s gives you that you'd otherwise build; if it's fewer than the operational tasks it adds, choose PaaS.
